```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, error = FALSE)
```

**Goal.** Fit a landscape conductance model to a pairwise genetic
distance matrix, such as $F_{ST}$, and read every part of the output. Use
this workflow when you start from distances rather than genotypes. If you
have not read
[`vignette("getting-started", package = "terradish")`](getting-started.html),
start there; it explains the conductance graph, and this guide covers what
changes when the response is a pairwise distance.

## When to use MLPE

MLPE, the maximum likelihood population effects model of Clarke, Rothery
and Raybould (2002), treats each pairwise genetic distance as a linear
function of the resistance distance between two sites:

$$D_{ij}=\alpha+\beta R_{ij}(\theta)+e_{ij}.$$

Here $R_{ij}(\theta)$ is the resistance distance through the conductance
graph, and the errors of two pairs that share a site, such as $(i,j)$ and
$(i,k)$, are correlated. That correlation is why ordinary regression on
pairwise distances overstates the evidence: the $n(n-1)/2$ pairs are not
independent observations. Use `measurement_model = mlpe` for $F_{ST}$,
$D_{PS}$, Nei's distance, or individual-based distances. Unlike the
Wishart models, MLPE needs no `nu`, because it estimates its own residual
variance.

## Load and inspect the data

The `melip` data hold pairwise $F_{ST}$ among 37 populations of
*Melipona* stingless bees in northeastern Brazil, with altitude and forest
cover rasters.

```{r data}
library(terradish)
library(terra)
data(melip)

# Rasters and points are stored wrapped; unwrap them before use.
altitude <- unwrap(melip.altitude)
forest <- unwrap(melip.forestcover)
coords <- unwrap(melip.coords)
Fst <- melip.Fst

c(sites = nrow(Fst), pairs = sum(lower.tri(Fst)),
  negative_pairs = sum(Fst[lower.tri(Fst)] < 0))
range(Fst[lower.tri(Fst)])
tryCatch(check_distance_response(Fst), error = conditionMessage)
```

**How to read the output.** There are 37 sites and 666 pairs. Two
$F_{ST}$ estimates are slightly negative, which unbiased estimators produce
when true differentiation is near zero. MLPE keeps them as they are.
`check_distance_response()` rejects the matrix because a valid squared
distance cannot be negative, so the Wishart distance model
`generalized_wishart` is not an option here; MLPE is.

## Build the conductance graph

```{r graph, warning = TRUE}
x <- c(forest, altitude)
names(x) <- c("forest", "altitude")
x <- scale_covariates(x)  # mean 0, SD 1; keeps the scaling for plot axes
surface <- conductance_surface(x, coords, directions = 8, saveStack = TRUE)
nrow(surface$x)  # number of raster cells in the graph
shared <- which(duplicated(surface$demes) | duplicated(surface$demes, fromLast = TRUE))
shared           # sites that fall in the same raster cell
```

**How to read the output.** The graph has
`r format(nrow(surface$x), big.mark = ",")` land cells. The warning flags
that `r length(shared)` sites fall in shared cells (three pairs), so the
resistance distance between each pair is zero. Their observed $F_{ST}$
values are small (0.01 to 0.06), so keeping them is reasonable here. With
your own data, use a finer raster or combine sites that share a cell.
These rasters are in longitude and latitude, so cells are about 5 km
across rather than a fixed distance; use a projected raster in your own
study.

## Fit candidate models

Fit a uniform-conductance baseline, a forest model, and a forest plus
altitude model to the same response and graph.

```{r fits}
control <- NewtonRaphsonControl(maxit = 200, ctol = 1e-8, ftol = 1e-8)
fit_ibd <- terradish(Fst ~ 1, surface, measurement_model = mlpe, control = control)
fit_forest <- terradish(Fst ~ forest, surface, measurement_model = mlpe, control = control)
fit_full <- terradish(Fst ~ forest + altitude, surface,
  measurement_model = mlpe, control = control)
aic_table(list(fit_ibd, fit_forest, fit_full),
          mod_names = c("IBD", "forest", "forest + altitude"))
```

**How to read the table.** `converged` must be `TRUE` for every model.
The uniform model is isolation by distance (IBD) on the graph: genetic
distance grows with separation, but every cell is equally easy to cross.
Lower AIC is better, and models within 2 units of the best have
comparable support. Forest improves on IBD by
`r round(AIC(fit_ibd) - AIC(fit_forest), 1)` AIC units, and adding
altitude improves on forest by a further
`r round(AIC(fit_forest) - AIC(fit_full), 1)`. MLPE is fitted by maximum
likelihood, not REML, so AIC can compare conductance formulas fitted to
the same distance matrix and graph.

## Read the MLPE summary

Start with the one-covariate model, where each part is easiest to see.

```{r summary}
summary(fit_forest)
```

The `Coefficients` table holds the conductance estimate. The
`Nuisance parameters` block holds the MLPE regression, on the scales
below.

| Parameter | Where it appears | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| `forest` (theta) | `coef(fit)` | Change in log conductance per SD of forest cover |
| `alpha` | `summary(fit)$phi` | Expected $F_{ST}$ at zero resistance distance |
| `beta` | `summary(fit)$phi` | Increase in $F_{ST}$ per unit of resistance distance |
| `tau` | `summary(fit)$phi`, log scale | Log residual precision; residual SD is `exp(-tau / 2)` |
| `rho` | `summary(fit)$phi`, logit scale | Shared-site correlation is `plogis(rho) / 2`, between 0 and 0.5 |

```{r interpret}
phi <- summary(fit_forest)$phi
sd_forest <- attr(x, "terradish_scale")$forest[["scale"]]
c(forest_SD = sd_forest,
  conductance_ratio = exp(coef(fit_forest)[["forest"]]),
  residual_sd = exp(-phi[["tau"]] / 2),
  shared_site_correlation = plogis(phi[["rho"]]) / 2)
exp(confint(fit_forest))  # 95% interval for the conductance ratio
```

**How to read the output.** One SD of forest cover is
`r round(sd_forest, 2)` (a proportion), and each SD increase multiplies
conductance by `r round(exp(coef(fit_forest)[["forest"]]), 2)`, with a 95%
interval of
`r paste(round(exp(confint(fit_forest)), 2), collapse = " to ")`.
`beta` (`r signif(phi[["beta"]], 2)`) is the slope of $F_{ST}$ on
resistance distance. Resistance distance has no fixed units, because the
model has no conductance intercept, so compare `beta` only within a fit.
`alpha` (`r signif(phi[["alpha"]], 2)`) is the intercept; a small negative
value is an extrapolation to zero resistance, not a predicted negative
$F_{ST}$ between real sites. The residual SD is about
`r signif(exp(-phi[["tau"]] / 2), 2)` in $F_{ST}$ units. The shared-site
correlation, `r round(plogis(phi[["rho"]]) / 2, 2)`, says how strongly
pairs involving the same population depart from the fitted line together;
values near the 0.5 ceiling mean site identity explains most of the
residual variation.

## Coefficients are conditional on the other terms

```{r full-model}
cbind(estimate = coef(fit_full), confint(fit_full))
anova(fit_forest, fit_full)
```

**How to read the output.** Once altitude enters, the forest coefficient
falls from `r round(coef(fit_forest)[["forest"]], 2)` to
`r round(coef(fit_full)[["forest"]], 2)` and its interval spans zero,
while altitude is strongly negative: higher cells conduct less. Each
coefficient is the association holding the other term fixed, and the two
estimates share information (their correlation is printed by
`summary(fit_full)`), so report them together rather than reading forest
alone. The likelihood-ratio test asks whether altitude improves on forest
alone; a chi-square of `r round(2 * as.numeric(logLik(fit_full) - logLik(fit_forest)), 1)`
on 1 degree of freedom is a large improvement in fit. Model-based
standard errors from MLPE tend to be optimistic, though, so check whether
the improvement holds for sites the model has not seen (below).

## Check the fit and map conductance

```{r fit-plot, fig.cap = "Observed versus fitted F~ST~ for every pair of sites under the forest plus altitude model."}
plot(fit_full, type = "fit")
```

**How to read the plot.** Each point is a pair of sites, with fitted
values on the horizontal axis. The blue line is a least-squares fit of
observed on fitted values, not the 1:1 line. Pairs share sites, so do not
treat the scatter as independent points or test the line's slope.

```{r marginal, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = c("Conductance across forest cover in the forest plus altitude model, averaged over the landscape's altitude values. The band is a 95% interval.", "Conductance across altitude, averaged over the landscape's forest values. Altitude is in the data's rescaled units (0 to about 1), not meters. The band is a 95% interval.")}
plot(fit_full, type = "marginal", data = surface)
```

```{r surface-map, fig.cap = "Fitted conductance under the forest plus altitude model, on a logarithmic color scale shared with its interval bounds."}
library(ggplot2)
C <- conductance(surface, fit_full)
maps <- plot(fit_full, type = "surface", data = surface)
maps[[1]] + scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10",
  limits = range(terra::values(C), na.rm = TRUE),
  name = "Conductance\n(log color scale)")
```

**How to read the curves and map.** Each curve varies one covariate and
averages conductance over the observed values of the other. Conductance
falls steeply with altitude and changes little with forest once altitude
is included. On the map, a cell at the landscape average of both
covariates has conductance 1, so values are relative to such a cell, and
equal color steps are equal ratios. `conductance(surface, fit_full)`
returns the estimate and its interval bounds as raster layers for your
own maps.

## Does the extra term predict new sites?

Cross-validation leaves out a spatial block of sites, fits each model to
the rest, and scores the held-out sites. `terradish_folds()` needs
projected coordinates to form spatial blocks, so project the points only
for this step.

```{r cv}
folds <- terradish_folds(project(coords, "EPSG:5880"), k = 4)
table(folds)
cv <- terradish_cv_folds(surface,
  list(IBD = Fst ~ 1, forest = Fst ~ forest, full = Fst ~ forest + altitude),
  folds = folds, model = mlpe, nuisance = "fixed", control = control)
cv$results[, c("model", "fold", "n_test", "loglik_gain", "error")]
cv$summary[, c("model", "n_folds_ok", "total_loglik", "mean_difference",
               "se_difference", "within_one_se")]
```

**How to read the output.** Each block holds 6 to 12 sites. With
`nuisance = "fixed"`, all parameters come from the training sites.
`loglik_gain` is the held-out improvement over the IBD model in the same
block; larger is better. The altitude model gains in three blocks but
loses `r round(abs(min(cv$results$loglik_gain)), 1)` units in block 3,
so its total falls below both simpler models, and all three are within
one standard error of the best (`within_one_se = TRUE`). The strong AIC
support for altitude therefore does not transfer reliably to new sites.
Report the altitude association as conditional and uncertain, and treat
forest's effect as not separable from altitude with these 37 sites.

## Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval = FALSE}
library(terradish)
library(terra)
data(melip)

# 1. Scale covariates and build the graph; keep scaling for plot axes.
x <- c(unwrap(melip.forestcover), unwrap(melip.altitude))
names(x) <- c("forest", "altitude")
surface <- conductance_surface(scale_covariates(x), unwrap(melip.coords),
  directions = 8, saveStack = TRUE)

# 2. Fit MLPE models to the pairwise distance matrix; no nu is needed.
ctl <- NewtonRaphsonControl(maxit = 200, ctol = 1e-8, ftol = 1e-8)
fits <- list(
  IBD = terradish(melip.Fst ~ 1, surface, measurement_model = mlpe, control = ctl),
  forest = terradish(melip.Fst ~ forest, surface, measurement_model = mlpe, control = ctl),
  full = terradish(melip.Fst ~ forest + altitude, surface,
    measurement_model = mlpe, control = ctl))
aic_table(fits, mod_names = names(fits))  # converged; Delta_AIC < 2 ties

# 3. Read one fit: conductance ratio and MLPE nuisance parameters.
summary(fits$forest)
exp(confint(fits$forest))                  # conductance ratio per SD
phi <- summary(fits$forest)$phi
exp(-phi[["tau"]] / 2)                     # residual SD (Fst units)
plogis(phi[["rho"]]) / 2                   # shared-site correlation

# 4. Nested test, diagnostics, and maps.
anova(fits$forest, fits$full)
plot(fits$full, type = "fit")
plot(fits$full, type = "marginal", data = surface)

# 5. Held-out prediction with spatial blocks (projected coordinates).
folds <- terradish_folds(project(unwrap(melip.coords), "EPSG:5880"), k = 4)
cv <- terradish_cv_folds(surface,
  list(IBD = melip.Fst ~ 1, forest = melip.Fst ~ forest,
       full = melip.Fst ~ forest + altitude),
  folds = folds, model = mlpe, nuisance = "fixed", control = ctl)
cv$summary
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `check_distance_response()` | Test whether a distance matrix is a valid squared distance for the Wishart models |
| `scale_covariates()` | Standardize raster layers and keep their scaling |
| `conductance_surface()` | Build the graph and locate the sampled sites |
| `terradish(..., measurement_model = mlpe)` | Fit conductance and MLPE parameters to a distance matrix |
| `aic_table()`, `anova()` | Compare models fitted to the same response and graph |
| `summary()`, `coef()`, `confint()` | Read conductance and MLPE nuisance estimates |
| `plot()`, `conductance()` | Diagnostics, conductance curves, and maps |
| `terradish_folds()`, `terradish_cv_folds()` | Spatial blocks and held-out prediction |

Clarke RT, Rothery P, Raybould AF (2002). Confidence limits for regression
relationships between distance matrices: estimating gene flow with
distance. *Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental
